title: Accenture Internship Process Experience
author: MANAV SINGLA
body:
The Accenture placement process consisted of five rounds, covering cognitive and behavioral skills, technical fundamentals, coding, communication, and a final interview.

Round 1: Behavioral & Cognitive Assessment

The first round was a combination of behavioral and cognitive assessment.

The behavioral section included questions based on workplace situations and personality traits. The cognitive section consisted of logical reasoning and puzzles, where we had to analyze the given situation and select the appropriate answer.

Preparation: Practice aptitude, logical reasoning, puzzles, and common behavioral questions.

Round 2: Technical Assessment

The second round was a technical assessment consisting mainly of MCQs based on Computer Science fundamentals.

The topics included:

Computer Networks

Basic Linux/command-line concepts

MS Excel

Programming fundamentals

Other basic CS concepts

This round mainly tested our understanding of fundamental technical concepts rather than advanced programming.

Preparation: Revise core CS subjects and practice MCQs covering networking, operating systems, databases, programming fundamentals, Excel, and basic commands.

Round 3: Coding Assessment

The third round was a coding assessment consisting of three different sections:

DSA: One basic Data Structures and Algorithms problem.

SQL: One SQL query based on database concepts.

Frontend: One question involving HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

For the coding question, the available languages were Java and Python; C++ was not available in my assessment.

The DSA problem was of basic difficulty, so understanding fundamental concepts and being comfortable with problem-solving was sufficient.

Preparation: Practice basic DSA problems, SQL queries, and fundamental HTML, CSS, and JavaScript concepts.

Round 4: Communication Assessment

The fourth round focused on English communication and listening skills.

It consisted of multiple activities, including:

Correcting grammatically incorrect sentences.

Speaking on a given topic for around one minute.

Listening to sentences and repeating them accurately.

Other exercises designed to evaluate communication and comprehension.

The main focus was on clarity, pronunciation, grammar, listening ability, and confidence while speaking.

Preparation: Practice speaking English on random topics for 1–2 minutes, improve basic grammar, and practice listening and repeating sentences.

Round 5: Virtual Interview

The final round was a virtual interview, which lasted approximately 15–20 minutes.

The interview mainly consisted of:

General HR questions.

Questions about my resume.

Discussion about projects.

Questions about my technical background and interests.

The questions were mostly straightforward, so having a good understanding of everything mentioned on your resume is important.

For HR preparation, resources such as InterviewBit and commonly asked HR interview questions can be useful.

After the OA, you have to wait.

title: Accenture AEH Intern Interview Experience
author: AARYAN RAJPUT
body:
My Accenture hiring experience had multiple rounds, and overall I would say the process was manageable if your basics were clear and you had knowledge across different areas.

The first round was an Ability + Aptitude assessment. It had a mix of mathematical aptitude, logical reasoning, and puzzle-based questions. Nothing felt extremely difficult, but time management was important because some questions and puzzles could take a little longer to solve.

After that, there was an MCQ round with around 40 questions. One important thing about this round was that the questions were spread across a lot of different topics rather than being focused on just one subject.

There were questions from CS fundamentals, databases, programming fundamentals, operating systems, DevOps, and even some questions related to AI and deep learning. So having knowledge across different fields definitely helps. You don't need to know every topic in extreme depth, but having a good understanding of the basics across different areas is useful.

The next round was the coding assessment. It wasn't only focused on DSA, which made it a little different from a typical coding round.

There were three types of questions:

One Data Structures/Programming problem, which I had to solve using Python.

One SQL problem, where we had to write a query according to the given requirements.

One frontend question, where we were provided with three files — index.html, styles.css, and script.js. We had to understand the existing code and make some basic changes according to the requirements.

I would recommend being comfortable with basic Python problem-solving, SQL queries, and HTML/CSS/JavaScript rather than preparing only DSA.

After the coding round, there was a communication assessment.

This round was fairly simple but had multiple sections. There were email-writing questions and grammar-based questions where a sentence had an error and we had to correct it.

There was also a repeat-the-sentence section where a sentence was played and we had to repeat it correctly.

Another section involved being given a topic with around 15 seconds to prepare, after which we had to speak about that topic for approximately 60 seconds. The topics were generally simple, so the main thing was being able to quickly organize your thoughts and communicate clearly.

After that came the interview round.

My interview was relatively simple and conversational. They asked me a few questions about my projects, but a large part of the interview focused on behavioral and situational questions around teamwork, leadership, and conflict resolution.

Some questions I remember were:

If one of your team members is not contributing properly, how would you handle the situation?

What role did you play in your last project?

What were the main technical difficulties you faced?

Was there a situation where you had to make a technical trade-off? Why did you make that decision?

What is the difference between an array, a set, a hash map, and a hash table?

For the project questions, I think it is much better to genuinely understand what you built instead of memorizing an explanation. Be prepared to talk about your contribution, the challenges you faced, the technical decisions you made, and any trade-offs you had to consider.

One unusual thing happened in my case after these rounds.

Most of the other candidates received their results before me, while my result did not clearly mention whether I was selected or rejected. Later, I was informed that there had been an error with my communication assessment.

Because of that, I was asked to take the communication assessment again. I completed it, and after that my process continued normally. Eventually, I was selected.

So one thing I would point out about Accenture is that the results can sometimes come at different times for different candidates. If other people receive their results before you and yours is still pending, it does not necessarily mean that you have been rejected.

Overall, my preparation advice would be to focus on aptitude, programming fundamentals, CS fundamentals, databases, operating systems, DevOps, basic AI/ML concepts, Python, SQL, frontend basics, communication skills, and your own projects.

The biggest takeaway from my experience is that Accenture's process tests you across a wide variety of areas. You don't have to be an expert in everything, but having good breadth of knowledge and being able to explain your projects and experiences clearly can help a lot.

title: Accenture AEH Internship Selection Experience
author: V SAI KIRAN REDDY
body:
I had a great experience with the Accenture selection process for the Advanced Application Engineering (AEH) Internship. Accenture visited our campus in December 2025, and I applied for the opportunity. The selection process was conducted in multiple stages and tested cognitive ability, technical knowledge, coding skills, communication, and interview performance.

1. Assessment Rounds

The first stage consisted of three assessments conducted on the same day, and these were elimination rounds.

Cognitive Assessment:

The cognitive assessment consisted of three game-based sections designed to test logical thinking, problem-solving, attention, and reasoning abilities. The games included Bubble Math, Key & Door, and a Path Finder-type game. The format was quite different from a traditional aptitude test and required quick thinking and accuracy.

Technical MCQ Assessment:

The technical round consisted of around 45 MCQs covering different areas of computer science and software development. The questions included pseudocode, computer fundamentals, web technologies, web development, and other technical concepts. A good understanding of CS fundamentals was important for this round.

Coding Assessment:

The coding assessment was divided into three sections:

Backend: Python, Java, or C#

Frontend: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

SQL: Database and SQL-related problems

This round tested both programming fundamentals and practical development knowledge.

One interesting aspect of the process was that the rounds were elimination-based, and candidates could know whether they had qualified for the next stage after completing the respective assessments.

I successfully cleared all three assessments and was shortlisted for the communication round.

2. Communication Assessment

The communication assessment was conducted a few days later. It focused on overall English communication skills and consisted of different sections covering Listening, Speaking, Reading, and Writing (LSRW) skills.

There was also an email-writing section, where communication and writing ability were evaluated. I successfully cleared this round as well.

3. Interview Round

Around a week after the communication assessment, I received the opportunity to appear for the interview.

The interview was primarily an HR-oriented round, along with a few technical questions from computer science fundamentals. The interviewer asked normal HR questions along with questions related to my technical background, projects, and CS concepts.

After successfully completing the interview, I was selected for the Accenture Advanced Application Engineering (AEH) Internship.

4. Internship and PPO

I completed the internship and subsequently received a Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) from Accenture for the Advanced Technology Engineer role, with a CTC of ₹13.6 LPA.

Thank you and All the best👍

-V Sai Kiran Reddy

After a crisp introduction, the interviewer dove into the architecture of my machine learning projects, probing not just what I built, but why I chose specific algorithms.

title: Recruitment Experience at Accenture
author: MANYA KAPOOR
body:
Recruitment Process Stages

The recruitment process for my Accenture internship consisted of multiple stages, with each round evaluating a different set of skills.

1. Registration & Application

I applied for the internship opportunity through my college placement process.

After the initial screening, I was eligible to proceed to the assessment rounds.

2. Cognitive & Technical Assessment

The next stage was an online assessment focused on:

Aptitude and logical reasoning

Verbal ability

Basic technical concepts

Fundamental programming and problem-solving skills

After completing the assessment, a confirmation window appeared indicating that I had successfully cleared the round and could proceed to the next stage.

3. Communication Assessment

After clearing the cognitive and technical assessment, I moved on to the communication round.

Once again, after completing the round, I received an on-screen confirmation stating that I had cleared the stage and qualified for the next round.

Clearing each stage one after another made the process feel very progressive, as every successful round brought me one step closer to the final selection stage.

4. Shortlisting for the Interview

After successfully clearing all the assessment rounds, I was finally shortlisted for the interview.

This was the last and most interactive stage of the recruitment process.

5. Final Interview Round

I had prepared my introduction very thoroughly, as I wanted to create a strong first impression.

I focused on making it:

Clear

Confident

Well-structured

Relevant to my academic background and experience

A major part of the interview revolved around my project experience.

I was asked about:

The objective of my project

The technologies I used

My individual contribution

The specific responsibilities I handled

How I approached challenges during the project

I was also given a situation-based question to assess how I would respond to a practical workplace scenario.

Another part of the discussion focused on leadership. I was asked how I would lead a team in a given situation.

Final Note

The process is quite manageable.

Just be confident about what you have done, know your projects well, and explain your contribution clearly.

The process was a little stressful initially because I was not completely sure what to expect in the interview. I prepared by revising my technical basics, going through my resume, and making sure I could explain my projects and technical skills clearly.

During the interview, I was asked questions related to my resume, projects. I also got questions about my internship interests and how I approach technical problems. The experience helped me understand the importance of being confident and clear while explaining my work.

One important thing I learned was that you should be completely honest about the skills and technologies you mention on your resume. It is better to have a clear understanding of a few technologies than to mention many things without being able to explain them.

My advice to other students would be to revise their basics, understand their projects properly, and practice explaining their resume before the interview. Staying calm and being honest when you don't know something can also make a big difference.

Overall, the Accenture selection experience helped me improve my technical preparation, communication skills, and confidence, and gave me a better understanding of how to approach internship interviews.

title: Accenture AEH-FTE Placement Experience
author: DURGESH KUMAR
body:
I’m happy to share that I got selected at Accenture for the role of Advanced Engineering Analyst (AEH). I wanted to share my experience to help juniors understand the process better and prepare in the right direction.

The hiring process consisted of multiple rounds:

Assessment 1: Behavioral & Cognitive (40 minutes)
This round mainly focused on personality-based and situational questions. Along with that, there were logical puzzles, number series, pattern recognition, and numerical reasoning questions. The key here is to stay calm and focus on accuracy rather than speed.

Assessment 2: Technical (45 minutes)
This section covered basic technical concepts like MS Office, common IT applications, and pseudocode (loops, conditions, flow). You should also be clear with networking basics (OSI, TCP/IP), cloud concepts (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS), and fundamental CS topics like arrays, functions, and OOPs.

Assessment 3: Coding (60 minutes)
There were 3 coding questions, and you could choose your preferred language or stack (Java, Python, C++, C#, SQL, or web stack). The questions ranged from easy to medium level, with one being more logic-based. Topics were mostly arrays, strings, loops, conditions, and basic SQL queries.

Assessment 4: Communication (~30 minutes)
This round evaluated spoken English, pronunciation, fluency, and listening skills. It also included grammar, vocabulary, and professional email writing.

Final Round: Interview
The interview was a mix of technical and HR questions. They asked questions based on my resume, discussed my projects in detail, and also included situational questions related to teamwork, adaptability, and strengths/weaknesses.

If you’re preparing for Accenture, make sure your basics are clear and practice regularly.
